From the EUR-Lex webpage for the GDPR; this chunk continues the language selector and gives the site's main navigation menu (EU law, Treaties, legal acts, case-law, Official Journal, and related EUR-Lex sections).

From the EUR-Lex webpage for the GDPR; this chunk continues the site menu and gives the document's metadata panel (procedure info, save/bookmark/permanent-link options, table of contents toggle, and the consolidated-version selector for the 04/05/2016 version), then begins the Regulation's official title.
From the EUR-Lex webpage for the GDPR; this chunk continues the Regulation's title and gives the page's language-format dropdowns (PDF, Official Journal, and multilingual display language selectors).
From the EUR-Lex webpage for the GDPR; this chunk continues the Regulation's title and gives the page's language-format dropdowns (PDF, Official Journal, and multilingual display language selectors).

From the GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679); this chunk finishes the Regulation's title and preamble (citing Article 16 TFEU and the legislative procedure) and opens the Recitals with recital (1) on data protection as a fundamental right through recital (4), which frames data protection as not absolute but balanced against other fundamental rights.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (5) on the economic and social integration driving increased cross-border personal data flows, recital (6) on technology enabling data collection/sharing at unprecedented scale, recital (7) on the need for a strong, coherent framework backed by trust, and recitals (8)-(9) on Member States specifying conditions and the fragmentation problems under Directive 95/46/EC that necessitated harmonisation.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (10) on ensuring a consistent, high level of protection while allowing Member States to maintain or introduce further conditions in specific areas (e.g. employment) and recital (11) on effective protection requiring strengthened data subject rights, controller/processor obligations, monitoring, and sanctions.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (12) on the Article 16(2) TFEU legal basis, recital (13) on ensuring a consistent level of protection and legal certainty across the internal market while accounting for SMEs, recital (14) on protection extending to natural persons regardless of nationality/residence (not legal persons), and recital (15) on the Regulation's technology neutrality.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (15) and covers recital (16) on the exclusion of national-security and CFSP activities, recital (17) on the separate but consistent Regulation applicable to EU institutions/bodies, recital (18) on the household/personal-activity exclusion, and recital (19) on the exclusion of processing by competent authorities for law-enforcement purposes (covered instead by the Law Enforcement Directive).
From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk gives recital (20) on the Regulation applying to courts and judicial authorities while safeguarding judicial independence.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (21) on the Regulation applying without prejudice to the e-Commerce Directive's intermediary liability rules, recital (22) on 'establishment' meaning effective and real exercise of activity, and recital (23) on the Regulation applying to controllers/processors outside the Union that offer goods/services to or monitor data subjects in the Union.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (24) on monitoring the behaviour of data subjects within the Union, recital (25) on application where Member State law applies by virtue of public international law, recital (26) on anonymised data falling outside the Regulation's scope, and recital (27) on the Regulation not applying to deceased persons' data (with Member States free to legislate otherwise).

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (24) on monitoring the behaviour of data subjects within the Union, recital (25) on application where Member State law applies by virtue of public international law, recital (26) on anonymised data falling outside the Regulation's scope, and recital (27) on the Regulation not applying to deceased persons' data (with Member States free to legislate otherwise).

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (27) tail, recital (28) on pseudonymisation reducing risks to data subjects, recital (29) on applying pseudonymisation within the same controller with additional safeguards, recital (30) on online identifiers like cookies and IP addresses potentially constituting personal data, recital (31) on public authorities receiving disclosures not being treated as 'recipients', and recital (32) on consent requiring a clear affirmative act.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (32) tail, recital (33) on the flexibility for consent in scientific research contexts, recital (34) on the definition of genetic data, and recital (35) on the definition of health data.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk gives recital (36) on determining a group's 'main establishment' by the location of effective and real management activities, and recital (37) on the definition of a 'group of undertakings' via a controlling undertaking.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (37) and gives recital (38) on children meriting specific protection given their lesser awareness of processing risks (including the age of consent for information-society services), and opens recital (39) on the principles of transparency, purpose limitation, and data minimisation.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (40) on lawful processing requiring a legal basis such as consent or contract, recital (41) on 'law' as a basis not necessarily requiring a legislative act but needing to be clear and foreseeable, and recital (42) on the burden of proof for consent, plain-language requirements, and the right of withdrawal.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (43) on consent not being freely given where there is a clear imbalance (e.g. public authorities or employers), recital (44) on the contractual-necessity legal basis, and recital (45) on the legal-obligation basis for processing.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (46) on the vital-interests legal basis for processing and recital (47) on the legitimate-interests basis and the balancing test against data subjects' interests and reasonable expectations.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (48) on legitimate interest for transmitting personal data within a group of undertakings for internal administrative purposes, recital (49) on network and information security as a legitimate interest, and recital (50) on further processing for a compatible purpose.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk gives recital (51) on special categories of personal data meriting higher protection due to their sensitivity and the fundamental-rights risks of their processing.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (52) on exceptions to the prohibition on processing special categories of data for substantial public-interest reasons, and recital (53) on processing health-related special-category data for public-health and healthcare-system purposes.
From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (53) and gives recital (54) on processing for public-health purposes such as protecting against cross-border health threats.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (55) on official-authority processing by state, constitutional, and religious bodies, recital (56) on processing personal data on political opinions by political parties without the data subject's consent for democratic-system purposes, recital (57) on the GDPR not applying where a controller cannot identify a data subject (linked to Article 11), recital (58) on the principle of transparency and plain language especially for information addressed to children, and the start of recital (59) on procedures for exercising data subject rights.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (59) (facilitating rights exercise, generally free-of-charge information) and gives recital (60) on the fair and transparent processing information duty, recital (61) on when information should be provided (at collection or within a reasonable period), and opens recital (62) on the exceptions to that information duty.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (62) (exceptions where the data subject already has the information, where it is impossible or disproportionately burdensome, or where disclosure is restricted by law) and gives recital (63) on the right of access to one's own data and health records, recital (64) on controllers using reasonable measures to verify the identity of a person exercising their rights, and opens recital (65) on the right to rectification and erasure ('right to be forgotten').

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (65) and gives recital (66) on strengthening the right to be forgotten online by requiring controllers to take reasonable steps, including technical measures, to inform other controllers to erase links or copies, and recital (67) on methods for restricting processing (e.g. temporarily removing data from a website).
From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk gives recital (68) on the right to data portability and its technical-feasibility limits.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (69) on the right to object requiring compelling legitimate grounds to override it, recital (70) on the explicit and separate right to object to direct-marketing processing, and recital (71) on the right not to be subject to solely automated decision-making with legal or significant effects, including the right to obtain human intervention.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (72) on profiling being subject to the GDPR's general rules on legal basis and principles (with EDPB guidance encouraged) and recital (73) on restrictions to rights and principles for objectives like national security, defence, and public security, consistent with the Charter and ECHR.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (74) on controllers' accountability and liability for their processing, recital (75) on risks to rights and freedoms varying in likelihood and severity, and recital (76) on assessing risk by reference to the nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (74) on controllers' accountability and liability for their processing, recital (75) on risks to rights and freedoms varying in likelihood and severity, and recital (76) on assessing risk by reference to the nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (76) and gives recital (77) on guidance for implementing appropriate measures and demonstrating compliance (via the Board, codes of conduct, certification) and recital (78) on data protection by design and by default, including pseudonymisation and data minimisation.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (79) on allocating responsibilities between joint controllers, recital (80) on the requirement for non-EU controllers to designate a representative in the Union, and recital (81) on selecting processors offering sufficient guarantees and governing processing through a contract.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (82) on maintaining records of processing activities to demonstrate compliance and recital (83) on implementing risk-based security measures, including encryption.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (84) on conducting a data protection impact assessment and prior consultation with the supervisory authority for high-risk processing, recital (85) on notifying personal data breaches to the supervisory authority, and recital (86) on notifying data subjects where a breach poses a high risk.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (87) on promptly determining whether a breach has occurred and notifying without undue delay, recital (88) on breach-notification procedures accounting for the nature and severity of the breach and any criminal investigations, and recitals (89)-(90) on replacing prior-checking notification requirements with risk-based data protection impact assessments, including for high-risk processing types.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (90) and gives recital (91) on large-scale processing operations requiring a data protection impact assessment and recital (92) on impact assessments covering a series of similar processing operations.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (92) and gives recital (93) on public authorities not needing a separate impact assessment where legal basis was already assessed, recital (94) on consulting the supervisory authority where an impact assessment indicates unmitigated high risk, recital (95) on the processor's duty to assist the controller, recital (96) on consultation with a group's data protection officer, and opens recital (97) on when a data protection officer must be designated.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (97) (DPO designation for public authorities, large-scale processing, or core activities involving regular systematic monitoring) and gives recital (98) on associations drawing up codes of conduct, recital (99) on submitting draft codes for supervisory-authority approval, recital (100) on encouraging certification mechanisms and seals, and opens recital (101) on international data transfers not undermining the level of protection.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (101) and gives recital (102) on the Union's power to conclude international agreements, recital (103) on Commission adequacy decisions for third countries/sectors, and recital (104) on the elements the Commission considers when assessing adequacy (rule of law, human rights, independent supervisory authorities, international commitments).

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (105) on the Commission also considering relevant international agreements when assessing adequacy, and recital (106) on the Commission monitoring and periodically reviewing adequacy decisions.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (107) on the Commission's power to decide that a third country no longer ensures an adequate level of protection and to amend, suspend, or repeal adequacy decisions, and recital (108) on using appropriate safeguards (binding corporate rules, standard contractual clauses, codes of conduct, certification) absent an adequacy decision.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (109) on using Commission- or supervisory-authority-adopted standard data protection clauses, recital (110) on supervisory-authority authorisation of contractual clauses or administrative arrangements, recital (111) on derogations for specific situations (explicit consent, contractual necessity, public interest, legal claims, vital interests), and opens recital (112) on derogations for important public-interest reasons and international agreements.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (112) and gives recital (113) on transfers qualified as occasional and not repetitive being limited to legitimate interests that do not override data subjects' interests, and opens recital (114) on Member States encouraging the development of transfer mechanisms and effective legal remedies absent an adequacy decision.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (114) and gives recital (115) on counteracting extraterritorial application of third-country laws contrary to international law, and recital (116) on the importance of transfers to third countries for enforcing data protection and cooperation between supervisory authorities.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (117) on establishing an independent supervisory authority in each Member State, recital (118) on the independence of supervisory authorities, recital (119) on Member States ensuring adequate resources for their supervisory authorities, recital (120) on general conditions for supervisory authority members, and recital (121) on providing supervisory authorities with financial, human, and technical resources, premises, and infrastructure.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (122) on each supervisory authority's territorial competence, recital (123) on supervisory authorities monitoring GDPR application and contributing to consistent application through cooperation, and recital (124) on the lead-authority mechanism for cross-border processing that substantially affects data subjects in more than one Member State (the 'one-stop-shop').

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (125) on the lead authority's decision being binding on other concerned supervisory authorities and enforceable in courts, recital (126) on the coherent exercise of tasks and powers under the consistency mechanism, and recital (127) on supervisory authorities still handling local complaints not substantially affecting data subjects in other Member States.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (128) on the one-stop-shop mechanism not applying to processing by public authorities or private bodies acting in the public interest, and recital (129) on ensuring supervisory authorities have equivalent investigative, corrective, authorisation, and advisory tasks and powers.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (130) on the lead authority informing other concerned supervisory authorities and the Board of a matter, and recital (131) on the urgency procedure allowing a concerned supervisory authority to adopt provisional measures.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (132) on awareness-raising activities directed at controllers/processors (especially SMEs) and the public, recital (133) on mutual assistance between supervisory authorities, recital (134) on the Board coordinating joint operations, recital (135) on the consistency mechanism ensuring uniform application, recital (136) on the Board taking into account consulted parties' views, and opens recital (137) on the urgent need to act to protect data subjects.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (137) and gives recital (138) on Board opinions/decisions generally requiring simple majority (two-thirds for urgent binding decisions), recital (139) on the Board's establishment as a Union body with legal personality, and recital (140) on the Board being assisted by a secretariat provided by the EDPS, opening recital (141) on the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority and to an effective judicial remedy.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (141) and gives recital (142) on a data subject's right to mandate a body or organisation to lodge a complaint on their behalf, and opens recital (143) on a person's right to bring an action before the courts of the Member State where the supervisory authority is established to seek annulment of its decision.
From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk continues recital (143) on judicial review of supervisory authority decisions and the procedures for bringing such actions before national courts.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (144) on courts contacting each other to confirm parallel proceedings concerning the same processing, recital (145) on jurisdiction for actions against a controller/processor (courts where the defendant is established or the data subject resides), and recital (146) on the controller's/processor's duty to compensate damage suffered, interpreted broadly to ensure full and effective compensation.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (147) on specific jurisdiction rules not affecting general procedural rules, recital (148) on penalties including administrative fines, with the option of a reprimand instead of a fine for minor infringements or where a fine would be a disproportionate burden on a natural person, and opens recital (149) on Member States laying down rules on criminal penalties for infringements not subject to administrative fines.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (149) and gives recital (150) on the amounts and imposition of administrative fines, and recital (151) on the Denmark/Estonia adaptation where fines are initiated by the supervisory authority but imposed by national courts.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (149) and gives recital (150) on the amounts and imposition of administrative fines, and recital (151) on the Denmark/Estonia adaptation where fines are initiated by the supervisory authority but imposed by national courts.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (155) on Member State law providing specific rules for the employment context (recruitment, contract performance, equality/diversity, health and safety, employer/customer property protection) and recital (156) on processing for archiving, scientific/historical research, and statistical purposes subject to appropriate safeguards and derogations.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (157) on combining registry information to obtain new knowledge and statistics benefiting research, and recital (158) on archiving in the public interest and records of enduring value.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (158) and gives recital (159) on the broad interpretation of scientific research purposes (technological development and demonstration, fundamental and applied research, privately funded research), recital (160) on historical research purposes including genealogical research, recital (161) on the applicability of the Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) 536/2014 to consent for clinical trials, and opens recital (162) on statistical purposes and statistical confidentiality under Union/national law.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (162) and gives recital (163) on protecting confidential information collected by statistical authorities, recital (164) on Member State law on supervisory-authority powers over controllers subject to professional secrecy obligations, recital (165) on respecting the status of churches and religious associations under national constitutional law, and opens recital (166) on delegated-act powers granted to the Commission regarding certification.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk finishes recital (162) and gives recital (163) on protecting confidential information collected by statistical authorities, recital (164) on Member State law on supervisory-authority powers over controllers subject to professional secrecy obligations, recital (165) on respecting the status of churches and religious associations under national constitutional law, and opens recital (166) on delegated-act powers granted to the Commission regarding certification.

From the Recitals of the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (167) on implementing powers for standard forms and information-exchange procedures, recital (168) on the examination procedure applying to implementing acts on standard contractual clauses and adequacy, recital (169) on immediate application of an implementing act where adequate protection has ceased, and recital (170) on Directive 95/46/EC's repeal while existing Commission/supervisory-authority decisions remain in force.

From the GDPR; this chunk covers recital (171) on the two-year transition period for processing already underway under Directive 95/46/EC, recital (172) on the EDPS's 2012 opinion, and recital (173) on the Regulation's relationship with the ePrivacy Directive, concluding the Recitals, then opens the operative text with 'HAVE ADOPTED THIS REGULATION' and Chapter I (General provisions), giving the full text of Article 1 (Subject-matter and objectives) and the start of Article 2's heading.

From Chapter I of the GDPR; this chunk gives the full text of Article 2 (Material scope, including the exclusions for activities outside Union law, CFSP, purely personal/household activity, and law-enforcement purposes, and the cross-reference to Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 for EU institutions) and opens Article 3 (Territorial scope) with paragraphs 1-2 on establishment-based and targeting/monitoring-based application.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 3 (Territorial scope, paragraph 3 on Member State law by virtue of public international law) and opens Article 4 (Definitions), giving the start of its numbered definitions list (e.g. 'personal data', 'processing').

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 3 (Territorial scope, paragraph 3 on Member State law by virtue of public international law) and opens Article 4 (Definitions), giving the start of its numbered definitions list (e.g. 'personal data', 'processing').
From Article 4 of the GDPR (Definitions); this chunk continues the numbered definitions list, covering terms such as 'controller', 'processor', 'third party', and 'consent'.
From Article 4 of the GDPR (Definitions); this chunk continues the numbered definitions list, covering terms such as 'controller', 'processor', 'third party', and 'consent'.

From Article 4 of the GDPR (Definitions); this chunk continues the numbered definitions list, covering terms such as 'personal data breach', 'genetic data', 'biometric data', 'health data', and 'main establishment'.

From Article 4 of the GDPR (Definitions); this chunk finishes the numbered definitions list (e.g. 'representative', 'enterprise', 'group of undertakings', 'binding corporate rules', 'supervisory authority') and opens Article 5 (Principles relating to processing of personal data), giving its principles such as lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, and data minimisation.

From Article 4 of the GDPR (Definitions); this chunk finishes the numbered definitions list (e.g. 'representative', 'enterprise', 'group of undertakings', 'binding corporate rules', 'supervisory authority') and opens Article 5 (Principles relating to processing of personal data), giving its principles such as lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, and data minimisation.

From Article 5 of the GDPR; this chunk finishes the data-processing principles (accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, and the controller's accountability for demonstrating compliance) and opens Article 6 (Lawfulness of processing), giving the start of its six legal bases (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public interest, legitimate interests).

From Article 6 of the GDPR (Lawfulness of processing); this chunk continues the conditions for relying on the legitimate-interests basis and the factors for assessing whether further processing for a new purpose is compatible with the original purpose (paragraph 4).

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 6 and opens Article 7 (Conditions for consent, covering the burden of proof, plain-language requirement, and right of withdrawal), before opening Article 8 (Conditions applicable to a child's consent in relation to information society services), giving the start of its age-of-consent rules.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 7 (consent conditions) and Article 8 (child's consent, including the reasonable-efforts verification requirement) and opens Article 9 (Processing of special categories of personal data), giving the general prohibition in paragraph 1 and the start of its listed exceptions in paragraph 2.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 7 (consent conditions) and Article 8 (child's consent, including the reasonable-efforts verification requirement) and opens Article 9 (Processing of special categories of personal data), giving the general prohibition in paragraph 1 and the start of its listed exceptions in paragraph 2.

From Article 9 of the GDPR (Processing of special categories of personal data); this chunk continues the list of exceptions to the special-category prohibition (e.g. explicit consent, employment/social security law, vital interests, substantial public interest, healthcare, public health, archiving/research purposes).

From Article 9 of the GDPR (Processing of special categories of personal data); this chunk continues the list of exceptions to the special-category prohibition (e.g. explicit consent, employment/social security law, vital interests, substantial public interest, healthcare, public health, archiving/research purposes).

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 9 and gives the full text of Article 10 (Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences, requiring official-authority control or specific authorisation) and Article 11 (Processing which does not require identification), before opening Article 12 (Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of data subject rights), giving the start of its provisions on concise, transparent, and accessible communication.

From Article 12 of the GDPR (Transparent information, communication and modalities); this chunk continues the rules on response timelines for data subject requests, the general free-of-charge principle (with exceptions for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests), and identity-verification safeguards.

From Article 12 of the GDPR; this chunk finishes its provisions and opens Article 13 (Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject), giving the start of the list of information controllers must provide at the point of collection (identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention period).

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 13 (including the exceptions to the information duty) and opens Article 14 (Information to be provided where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject), giving the parallel information-provision list and its timing rules.

From Article 14 of the GDPR (Information where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject); this chunk continues the exceptions to this information duty (e.g. where the data subject already has the information, providing it is impossible or would involve disproportionate effort, or is required to remain confidential under professional secrecy).

From Article 14 of the GDPR (Information where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject); this chunk continues the exceptions to this information duty (e.g. where the data subject already has the information, providing it is impossible or would involve disproportionate effort, or is required to remain confidential under professional secrecy).

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 14 and opens Article 15 (Right of access by the data subject), giving the list of information a controller must confirm and provide upon an access request (purposes, categories of data, recipients, retention period, right to lodge a complaint, source of data, and existence of automated decision-making).

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 15 (the right to obtain a copy of personal data and safeguards for third-country transfers) and gives the full text of Article 16 (Right to rectification), before opening Article 17 (Right to erasure, the 'right to be forgotten'), giving the grounds on which a data subject can request erasure.

From Article 17 of the GDPR (Right to erasure); this chunk continues the erasure grounds, the controller's obligation to inform other controllers processing publicly available data to erase links/copies, and the exceptions to the right to erasure (e.g. freedom of expression, legal obligations, public interest, archiving/research purposes, legal claims).

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 17 and gives the full text of Article 18 (Right to restriction of processing, including its grounds and the notification-before-lifting-restriction rule) and opens Article 19 (Notification obligation regarding rectification, erasure, or restriction to each recipient the data was disclosed to).

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 19 and gives Article 20 (Right to data portability, including the conditions for its exercise and its non-applicability to public-task processing) and opens Article 21 (Right to object), giving the start of the objection grounds for legitimate-interest and direct-marketing processing.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 21 (the right to object, including its absolute character for direct marketing and its application to research/statistical purposes) and gives the full text of Article 22 (Automated individual decision-making, including profiling), covering the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions and its exceptions.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 22 and opens Article 23 (Restrictions), giving the list of important objectives (national security, defence, public security, other public interests, judicial independence, etc.) that can justify Member State or Union law restricting data subject rights and principles.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 23 and gives the full text of Article 24 (Responsibility of the controller, requiring appropriate technical/organisational measures and, where proportionate, adherence to codes of conduct or certification) and opens Article 25 (Data protection by design and by default), giving the start of its requirements.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 25 (data protection by design/default, including the certification-mechanism reference) and gives the full text of Article 26 (Joint controllers, requiring an arrangement determining respective responsibilities) and opens Article 27 (Representatives of controllers or processors not established in the Union), giving its designation requirements and exemptions.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 27 and opens Article 28 (Processor), giving the start of the requirements for a controller-processor contract (sufficient guarantees, documented instructions, confidentiality, sub-processor authorisation, and assistance obligations).

From Article 28 of the GDPR (Processor); this chunk continues the required contractual terms between controller and processor, including data deletion/return obligations at the end of provision of services and audit rights.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 28 and gives the full text of Article 29 (Processing under the authority of the controller or processor) and opens Article 30 (Records of processing activities), giving the start of the required record content for controllers.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 28 and gives the full text of Article 29 (Processing under the authority of the controller or processor) and opens Article 30 (Records of processing activities), giving the start of the required record content for controllers.

From Article 30 of the GDPR (Records of processing activities); this chunk continues the required record content for processors and the exemption for organisations with fewer than 250 employees (subject to certain conditions).

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 30, gives the full text of Article 31 (Cooperation with the supervisory authority) and Article 32 (Security of processing, including pseudonymisation/encryption and the risk-based approach), and opens Article 33 (Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority), giving its 72-hour notification deadline and required content.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 33 and gives the full text of Article 34 (Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject, including its high-risk trigger and exceptions), before opening Article 35 (Data protection impact assessment).

From Article 35 of the GDPR (Data protection impact assessment); this chunk covers the circumstances requiring a DPIA (in particular systematic profiling, large-scale special-category processing, or large-scale public monitoring) and the required content of the assessment.

From Article 35 of the GDPR (Data protection impact assessment); this chunk continues its provisions, including consulting the data protection officer, considering data subjects' views, and the exemption where a DPIA has already been carried out for similar processing.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 35 and opens Article 36 (Prior consultation), giving the requirement to consult the supervisory authority before processing where a DPIA indicates unmitigated high risk, and the supervisory authority's response timeline and powers.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 36 and opens Article 37 (Designation of the data protection officer), giving the circumstances requiring a DPO (public authorities, large-scale regular/systematic monitoring, or large-scale special-category processing) and related provisions.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 37 and gives the full text of Article 38 (Position of the data protection officer, covering independence, resources, and reporting to the highest management level) and opens Article 39 (Tasks of the data protection officer), listing the DPO's core duties.

From the GDPR; this chunk finishes Article 38 and Article 39 (the DPO's tasks, including informing/advising, monitoring compliance, and acting as contact point for the supervisory authority) and opens Article 40 (Codes of conduct), giving the start of the list of topics such codes may address.

From Article 40 of the GDPR (Codes of conduct); this chunk continues the list of topics codes of conduct may cover (fair processing, legitimate interests, breach notification, transfers, dispute resolution) and the submission/approval procedure.
